problems.label: Worry that is hard to switch off and fills much of the day
definitions: Reports spending an hour or more on most days worrying about several life areas, such as health, money, work or family, often about outcomes that are unlikely.
Has trouble finishing tasks or following conversations because worry keeps pulling attention away, by self or collateral report.
Lies awake going over worries, or keeps returning to the same worry many times in one day.
Describes the worry as hard to set aside even when they can see it is out of proportion to the actual risk.
longTermGoals: Worry takes up much less of the client's day, and the client can set a worry aside and bring attention back to the task in front of them.
The client can tell the difference between a problem they can act on and a what-if worry, and responds to each in a way that helps.

shortTermObjectives.text: For the next 2 weeks, log worry at least 3 times a day (topic, estimated minutes spent, distress 0-10) to set a baseline for daily worry time.
From week 3, postpone worries to one set 15 to 20 minute worry period on at least 5 days a week, aiming to cut estimated daily worry time to half of the baseline or less by week 8.

By week 5, sort at least 5 logged worries into 'problems I can act on now' and 'what-if worries I cannot solve today', and work through a structured problem-solving sheet for at least 1 actionable problem each week.
Over weeks 4 to 10, complete at least 2 thought records per week on worry predictions, rating how likely the feared outcome seems before and after, and later noting whether it actually happened.

Complete the GAD-7 at intake and every 2 to 4 weeks, plus the PHQ-9 at intake to check for low mood (repeating it on the same schedule if it is raised). Review the score trend together, and revisit the plan, the intensity of treatment or referral options if scores have not improved across 2 check-ins in a row.

problems.label: Ongoing physical tension, restlessness and broken sleep
definitions: Reports tight or sore muscles (jaw, neck or shoulders), tension headaches, or a wound-up feeling and trouble sitting still on most days.
Takes more than 30 minutes to fall asleep, or wakes and cannot get back to sleep, on 3 or more nights a week because of worry or tension.
Runs low on energy by midday, or snaps at family or coworkers more often than usual, by self or collateral report.
longTermGoals: The client notices tension early, can bring it down within a few minutes in everyday situations, and wakes feeling more rested.

shortTermObjectives.text: Within 2 weeks, name at least 3 personal early body signs of building tension (for example a clenched jaw, shallow breathing or raised shoulders) and note in a daily log when each one shows up.
Over the next 3 weeks, practice full progressive muscle relaxation for 15 to 20 minutes on at least 5 days a week, rating tension 0-10 before and after each session.

Over weeks 4 to 10, work with the clinician through shorter relaxation steps (release-only, cue-controlled and rapid versions) until the client can relax noticeably in about a minute, then use the quick version at least 5 times a day when early tension signs appear.
For 2 weeks, practice slow belly breathing for 5 minutes twice a day, and use it before at least 1 expected stressful moment each day.

For 4 weeks, keep a wake-up time that varies by no more than 30 minutes, move worrying and planning out of bedtime and into the daytime worry period, and log minutes to fall asleep each morning. If sleep has not improved by week 6, discuss a referral for cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia or a medical review.

problems.label: Checking, over-preparing and steering away from uncertainty
definitions: Asks others for reassurance about the same concern several times a day or week, or repeatedly checks messages, news or plans to feel calmer.
Over-prepares, for example rereading an email many times, drawing up detailed backup plans or researching a small purchase for hours.
Puts off decisions, new situations, test results or hard conversations because the outcome cannot be known in advance.
longTermGoals: The client makes everyday decisions and tries new things without first needing to feel sure of how they will turn out.

shortTermObjectives.text: Within 3 weeks, list at least 8 checking, reassurance or avoidance habits and rate how uneasy it would feel (0-100) to skip each one.

Over weeks 4 to 12, carry out at least 3 planned uncertainty practices a week (for example sending an email after one read-through or choosing a restaurant without checking reviews), writing down the feared result and what actually happened.
By week 8, cut reassurance-seeking about any single topic to once a day or less, tracked with a simple daily tally.
By week 10, use a step-by-step problem-solving method to make at least 2 decisions that had been put off, each within a time limit agreed in session.
In the final 2 sessions, write a short plan naming the skills that helped most, at least 3 signs that worry is creeping back and when to ask for a booster session.

collaborativeNote: These are starting points for clinician review, not a finished plan. Rewrite each goal and objective with the client in their own words, check that the practice amounts fit their schedule and energy, and record their agreement before anything is added to the plan. Separate realistic concerns that call for practical help (for example money, housing or immigration stress) from worry that is out of proportion, and adjust relaxation work for pain, injury, pregnancy or trauma history. Do not add names or other identifying details. Resource only. Not a substitute for clinical judgment.
